title: Rook behind the passed pawn
summary: Tarrasch's rule: the rook belongs behind the passed pawn, yours and your opponent's. And when the rule fails.
part.own.title: Behind your own pawn
part.own.summary: The rook behind the pawn ties down the black rook, and the king walks to b7.
part.front.title: In front of your own pawn
part.front.summary: With your rook in front of the pawn, Black holds; if Black's king leaves its post, there is a trick.
part.race.title: Getting behind in time
part.race.summary: A race of tempi: close the rank of the check, or gain the tempo with a check.
part.theirs.title: Behind the enemy pawn
part.theirs.summary: In defence the rook also goes behind the pawn; in front of it, the rook is tied down.
part.twoPassers.title: Two passers: Kramnik vs Beliavsky
part.twoPassers.summary: When the opponent's passer is the danger, the rook goes after it, not behind yours.
part.enemyBehind.title: His rook behind your pawn
part.enemyBehind.summary: Before promoting, take the rook behind out of play: drive its king away or block the file.
part.exceptions.title: When the rook works from the side
part.exceptions.summary: With your king in front of the pawn, or with two pawns, the rook does more from the side.
part.rules.title: Switching targets and the practical challenge
part.rules.summary: With the black rook tied down, the king goes after the pawns on the other side.
step.t_behind: You play White and have a passed pawn on the a-file. Look at where each rook stands: yours behind the pawn, the black one in front of it. What is your plan to win?
step.t_behind.hint1: Compare the two rooks. How many squares does each have on the a-file, and how many will it have when the pawn advances?
step.t_behind.hint2: The black rook cannot leave the front of the pawn. So your king is the one who helps the pawn, and Black has only the king to defend both the pawn and the kingside.
step.behind: Your rook is behind the pawn, the black rook is in front of it. Look at the difference. With every step the pawn takes, your rook gains one more square on the file and keeps protecting the pawn. The black rook does the opposite: it loses squares. With the pawn on a7 it has only a8, and if it leaves, the pawn queens. One rook has become a guard; the other is free.
step.d_walk: Watch how White wins. The idea is simple: the black rook is tied down, so your king walks to the pawn.
step.d_walk.m1: 1.a7! The pawn advances and the black rook is pinned to a8. If it leaves the file, the pawn queens with your rook's protection.
step.d_walk.m2: 1...Kf7. The black rook cannot leave a8; only the black king moves.
step.d_walk.m3: 2.Kf3. Your king sets off for the queenside. The white rook stays put: it is already doing its job.
step.d_walk.m4: 2...Kg7. Black guards the g6 pawn. If the black king ran to the queenside, your king would go and capture g6.
step.d_walk.m5: 3.Ke4. The target is b7: from there the king attacks the black rook.
step.d_walk.m6: 3...Kf7. Black has no useful move: the rook is stuck on a8, and the king just goes back and forth.
step.d_walk.m7: 4.Kd5. Two more moves, to c6 and b7, and nothing blocks the way.
step.d_walk.m8: 4...Ke7. The black king tries to come back to the queenside, but it is late.
step.d_walk.m9: 5.Kc6. The white king arrives first and watches b7 and c7.
step.d_walk.m10: 5...Kd8. The black king cannot step onto c7, which the white king watches, and cannot reach b7.
step.d_walk.m11: 6.Kb7 attacks the rook. It has to leave a8, and the pawn promotes with your rook's support. Notice that the white rook never had to move: behind the pawn, it works while standing still.
step.alekhine: This technique decided a world title. Buenos Aires, 1927, game 34 of the match between Alekhine and Capablanca. In the middlegame Alekhine's queen captured the a7 and b7 pawns (24.Qxa7 and 26.Qxb7), and the queens came off with 49...Qxd4 50.Rxd4. With 54.Ra4 the rook went behind the a-pawn, and Capablanca's rook was stuck on a6, in front of it. The white king walked to c3. When the kings blocked each other, Alekhine played 59.Ra2, a waiting move, and with 62.Kd4 he switched targets: he went after the kingside pawns. Capablanca resigned after 82.Re7, and Alekhine became world champion.
step.b7Race: Now the black king is close to the pawn, on c4, and the black rook will try to give checks. Win the race to b7.
step.b7Race.hint: The black king also wants to get close to the pawn. Take your king along a route where it arrives first, without running into the black king.
step.b7Race.done: 1.Kd6! Your king won the race. The black rook gave a check, but in front of the pawn it has nothing else to do: with the white king on b7, it has to leave a8, and the pawn promotes.
step.t_skewer: Now your rook stands in front of the b-pawn, and the black rook, behind it, attacks it. If your rook leaves the b-file without a threat, the pawn falls. But the black king is on e7, far from g7 and h7. How can you exploit that?
step.t_skewer.hint1: Where can your rook go on the 8th rank and still protect the promotion square?
step.t_skewer.hint2: If the black rook captures the pawn, it ends up on the 7th rank, the same as the black king.
step.front: First, the defensive set-up. The same pieces as at the start of the lesson, with the rooks swapped: your rook stands in front of the pawn and blocks its own pawn. The black rook, behind it, attacks the pawn and checks your king from a distance if it comes closer. Black keeps the king on g7 or h7 and waits: from there the king watches g8 and h8, and your rook has no way to leave the front of the pawn with a threat. It is a draw. Now back to the b-pawn position: there the black king has left g7.
step.d_skewer: See what happens when the black king leaves g7 and h7.
step.d_skewer.m1: 1.Rh8! The rook leaves the front with a threat: 2.b8=Q. From h8 it still protects b8 along the 8th rank.
step.d_skewer.m2: 1...Rxb7. The black rook captures the pawn, but now it is on the 7th rank, the same as the king.
step.d_skewer.m3: 2.Rh7+. Check, and the black rook is behind the king on the same rank: it is the skewer, and the rook falls.
step.frontCheck: Now the black king is on e6. The skewer along the 7th rank no longer works: if the black rook captures the pawn, the king is not on the same rank. Find another way out of the front with a threat.
step.frontCheck.hint: Look for a rook move that forces Black to respond before capturing the pawn.
step.frontCheck.done: 1.Re8+! The rook left the front with check, and from e8 it protects b8. After 2.b8=Q Rxb8 3.Rxb8, your rook remains. That is why Black keeps the king on g7 or h7.
step.t_race: Now your rook is not yet behind the a-pawn. It wants to go there, and so does the black rook: whoever arrives first decides. Which way does your rook go? The position comes from a study by Audax6.
step.t_race.hint1: Count the moves both rooks need to reach the a-file.
step.t_race.hint2: The black rook can get there with a check. Along which rank?
step.raceCount: Count the moves of both rooks. The black one reaches a2 in two, and the first is a check on f2, which gains it the tempo it needs. That is why the route that looks shortest can arrive too late.
step.d_raceError.m1: 1.Rc3? The rook seems on its way to a3, but it arrives too late.
step.d_raceError.m2: 1...Rf2+. The black rook checks along the 2nd rank and gains a tempo.
step.d_raceError.m3: 2.Kg3. The king steps out of check and attacks the rook, but it is already leaving.
step.d_raceError.m4: 2...Ra2. The black rook got behind the pawn before yours: now it attacks the pawn, and the good rook is Black's. It is a draw.
step.getFirst: Your turn: get behind the pawn before the black rook does.
step.getFirst.hint: Close the rank the black rook would use to give check.
step.getFirst.done: 1.Rc2! The rook closed the 2nd rank, and with 2.Ra2 it got behind the pawn first. Now it is the position you already know: the black rook stuck in front of the pawn and your king free to walk.
step.d_tempo: Sometimes you are a tempo short and there is no rank to close. Here 1.Ra1 does not work: your king on a2 is in the way, and 1...Rxa5+ captures the pawn with check.
step.d_tempo.m1: 1.Rd4+! The check forces the black king to move: that is the missing tempo.
step.d_tempo.m2: 1...Kg5. In check, Black has no time to capture a5: the king has to move first.
step.d_tempo.m3: 2.Ra4. The rook got behind the pawn, which is now protected. The black rook will have to stay in front of it.
step.tempoMove: The same idea on the other side of the board: bring the rook behind the h-pawn.
step.tempoMove.hint: The rook cannot get behind the pawn in one move. What forces Black to lose a move?
step.tempoMove.done: 1.Re4+! The check gained the tempo, and with 2.Rh4 the rook got behind the pawn.
step.t_defend: Now Black has the passed pawn and you defend. The a-pawn is protected by the black rook. Where should your rook go?
step.t_defend.hint1: Think of the rule you just saw. It works for both sides.
step.t_defend.hint2: Blockading the pawn looks safe, but look at what your rook would do there: nothing. Find the way to the square behind the pawn.
step.d_defend: The rook goes behind the pawn: from there it attacks it.
step.d_defend.m1: 1.Rd8. The rook sets off for a8, behind the pawn.
step.d_defend.m2: 1...a3. The pawn advances and moves away from the black rook, which protected it from c4.
step.d_defend.m3: 2.Ra8. Behind the pawn, the rook attacks a3, and the black rook on c4 no longer protects it. Now it is the black rook that has to look after the pawn, while yours attacks it from behind without being tied to it: a draw.
step.passive: And what if the rook blockades the pawn with 1.Ra1? Your rook is tied to the front of the pawn: if it leaves the a-file, the pawn runs. The black rook is free, and the black king walks to the pawn, with 1...Kf6 and then via e5 and d4, to push it. Black wins. A rook in front of the pawn is passive, whoever it belongs to.
step.anand: It is the same among grandmasters. Mexico City, 2007, round 3 of the tournament for the world title. With 35...Rxa3 Kramnik captured a pawn and was left with a passer on the a-file, with his rook in front of it. Anand did not try to blockade: after 36.Kf2 h5 37.g3 a5, he took the rook behind the pawn with 38.Ra7. The pawn reached a2 but got no further: after 59.Ra7 Rc1 60.Rxa2 Rc2+ 61.Rxc2 Kxc2, the rooks came off, and the king and pawn ending was drawn on move 65.
step.holdBehind: Now on the other side: bring the rook behind the h-pawn.
step.holdBehind.hint: The rook has to reach the h-file from behind the pawn. Which rank is free all the way there?
step.holdBehind.done: 1.Re8 and 2.Rh8: behind the pawn, the rook attacks it, and the pawn does not get through. A draw.
step.t_kramnik: Groningen, 1993, PCA tournament. You play Kramnik's white pieces. In the rook ending Kramnik captured the a7 and b5 pawns (48.Rxa7+ and 53.Rxb5), and Beliavsky captured g2 and h2 (46...Bxg2 and 52...Rxh2). Now your a-pawn is passed, and Black has the f- and h-pawns, with the king and rook next to them. The rule sends the rook behind your pawn. Does it apply here?
step.t_kramnik.hint1: Which pawn is closer to queening, and who is escorting it?
step.t_kramnik.hint2: Behind the a-pawn, the rook protects the a-pawn. And who will stop the f- and h-pawns?
step.kramnik: Kramnik played 59.Ra1?, behind his own pawn, as the rule says, and lost. There followed 59...Rg3+ 60.Kf2 Kg4: the white king was pushed back, and the black king stood next to its pawns. The a-pawn was far from promotion; the black pawns, with the king and rook close by, advanced together, and Beliavsky won on move 81.
step.rb8: What held was 59.Rb8! The rook gives up the a-pawn and goes behind the black pawns: from there it checks the black king and attacks the h-pawn. 59.Rb7 and 59.Rb6 also held, for the same reason. Botvinnik had already shown, in the 1940s, that rook and f- and h-pawns against rook is a draw with correct defence.
step.kramnikMove: Now the rook: put it where it saves the game.
step.kramnikMove.hint: The rook has more work to do against the black pawns than behind yours.
step.kramnikMove.done: 59.Rb8! The rook went behind the black pawns and checks from there, as with 60.Rg8+ and 61.Rh8+. Tarrasch's rule also applies to the opponent's passer, and here it was the black pawns that mattered.
step.t_order: The black rook is behind your a-pawn, and the black king is right next to your kingside pawns. Pushing the pawn looks natural, but think about the black rook's check along the 2nd rank and where the black king would go next. What do you play first?
step.t_order.hint1: Where does the black king go when your king steps out of check?
step.t_order.hint2: Before pushing the a-pawn, drive the black king away from your kingside.
step.orderWhy: Before pushing, look at your kingside. The black king on f4 is one step from g3: if a check drives your king to the 1st rank, the black king walks in there and traps it far from the pawn.
step.d_orderError: See what happens if the pawn advances at once.
step.d_orderError.m2: 1...Ra2+. The rook behind checks along the 2nd rank.
step.d_orderError.m3: 2.Kg1. The king steps out of check; e1 or f1 would not help either.
step.d_orderError.m4: 2...Kg3. The black king has entered your kingside: it attacks g2 and traps your king on the 1st rank. Your king has no way to reach the pawn, and Black holds.
step.orderMove: Now the right order: first deal with the black king, then the pawn.
step.orderMove.hint: A move that forces the black king away from your kingside.
step.orderMove.done: 1.g3+! The check pushed the black king away from your kingside, and only then came 2.a7. Now your king is not trapped on the 1st rank and can walk to the pawn.
step.d_interfere: Another weapon against the rook behind: blocking the file. Before promoting, take the rook behind out of play; in the previous position the pawn check drove the black king away, here your rook gets in the way. Here 1.d8=Q does not work: 1...Rxd8 and the pawn is gone.
step.d_interfere.m1: 1.Rh5! It threatens 2.Rd5, stepping between the black rook and the pawn.
step.d_interfere.m3: 2.Kd6. The king comes closer to the pawn and now protects d5.
step.d_interfere.m4: 2...Rd1+. One more check, along the d-file.
step.d_interfere.m5: 3.Rd5. The rook blocks the file and the check, protected by the king: if 3...Rxd5, 4.Kxd5 and the pawn queens.
step.interfereMove: The same idea, on the other side. Do not rush to promote.
step.interfereMove.hint: The black rook only holds the pawn along its file. Prepare a square to block that file, close to your king.
step.interfereMove.done: 1.Ra5! The rook went to the 5th rank and, after the checks, 3.Re5 blocked the file, protected by the king. The pawn promotes.
step.t_kingFront: Your king stands in front of your own h-pawn, and the pawn cannot move while the king is there. The rule sends the rook behind the pawn, to h2. What would it do there? Where does the rook work best?
step.t_kingFront.hint1: The danger is the black king getting close to the pawn. Which way would it come?
step.t_kingFront.hint2: A rook can bar a whole king's way along a rank.
step.kfError: So far the rook has gone behind the pawn. Now, two cases where it does more from the side. First the rule's move, 1.Rh2? The rook behind the pawn does nothing: the pawn cannot move, because your king is in front of it. Meanwhile the black king comes with 1...Kf5 and reaches f6, right next to the pawn and your king. It is a draw.
step.d_kf: The right move cuts off the black king.
step.d_kf.m1: 1.Rc5! The rook closes the 5th rank: the black king cannot cross to the pawn's side.
step.d_kf.m2: 1...Kf4. The black king looks for another way, but the 5th rank stays closed.
step.d_kf.m3: 2.Kh7. Your king steps out from in front of the pawn.
step.kfMove: Your turn: cut off the black king and free the pawn.
step.kfMove.hint: Close the rank the black king would come through.
step.kfMove.done: 1.Rf5! The rook cut off the black king, and 2.Ka7 took your king out from in front of the pawn.
step.d_sideGuard: Another exception: two passed pawns. If the rook goes behind the a-pawn, with 1.Ra1, it protects only that pawn, and 1...Kxf5 draws.
step.d_sideGuard.m1: 1.Rd5! From the 5th rank the rook protects a5 and f5 at the same time.
step.d_sideGuard.m2: 1...Kf4. The black king comes closer to attack the rook.
step.d_sideGuard.m4: 2...Ke4. The black king attacks the rook on d5.
step.d_sideGuard.m5: 3.Rb5. The rook steps out of the attack and stays on the 5th rank, protecting both pawns.
step.sideGuardMove: Your turn: protect both pawns at once.
step.sideGuardMove.hint: Look for the rank both pawns stand on.
step.sideGuardMove.done: 1.Rc5! The rook guards both pawns from the side, and the black rook stays tied to the a-pawn. After 1...Ra6, 2.Kg2 brings the king up.
step.tarrasch: Siegbert Tarrasch, one of the great German masters of the early twentieth century, wrote in the book of the St. Petersburg 1914 tournament that rooks belong behind passed pawns: behind your own to support the advance, behind the opponent's to hinder it. The reason is the one you have just seen: the rook behind gains room with every step of the pawn, the rook in front loses it. He admitted exceptions himself; he is quoted as saying: always put the rook behind the pawn, except when that is wrong.
step.recap: Three rules to take to your games. One: the rook goes behind the passed pawn, yours and your opponent's. Two: getting behind is a race; close the rank of the check or gain the tempo with a check. Three: before following the rule, ask what the rook does there: with your king in front of the pawn, with two pawns to protect, or with the opponent's passer more dangerous, it works from the side or against the other pawn.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge, from the position at the start of the lesson. Keep the rook behind the pawn, bring the king forward and win. If the black king runs to the a-pawn, switch targets.
ex.e05: White to move and win. The black rook stands in front of the pawn. How do you exploit that?
ex.e05.hint: The white king wants to reach b7. What stops it right now?
ex.e05.solution: 1.Rb2+! The check drives the black king off the b-file. After 1...Ka6, 2.Kc7! and the white king reaches b7: the black rook, in front of the pawn, cannot guard a8 and give checks at the same time. Beware of 2.Kc6, which looks the same and only draws. Idea from a study by SHREKDAVID.
ex.e06: White to move and win. Your rook is in front of the pawn, but the black king has left the right square. Punish the mistake.
ex.e06.hint: Free the a8 square with a threat. What happens if the black rook takes the pawn?
ex.e06.solution: 1.Rh8! It threatens 2.a8=Q. If the rook takes the pawn, 2.Rh7+ skewers king and rook along the seventh rank. With the black king on g7 or h7 this trick does not exist: that is why Black keeps the king there.
ex.e11: White to move and win. The rook is not behind the pawn yet, and the black rook is already eyeing a6. Where should your rook stand, and how does it get there in time?
ex.e11.hint: In front of the pawn the rook only draws. To get behind it you need a spare tempo. Who can give it to you?
ex.e11.solution: 1.Rc5+! The check gains the tempo, and next move 2.Ra5 puts the rook behind the pawn, guarding a6. Without the check, the black rook takes the pawn first. 1.Ra8, in front of it, only draws: after 2.a7 the black rook gets behind the pawn on the a-file and checks your king. Position from a study by miles26.
ex.e10: White to move and win. Here the rule misleads: the rook behind the h-pawn only draws. Find the winning move.
ex.e10.hint: Your king is stuck in front of its own pawn. What stops the black king from coming closer?
ex.e10.solution: 70.Rf7! The rook cuts the black king off along the f-file, and the white king gets out of the pawn's way. 70.Rf6, 70.Rf1 and 70.Rf2 also win. In Short against Yusupov, 1984, White played 70.Rh3, behind the pawn, and the game was drawn.
ex.e12: White to move and draw. Each side has a passed pawn, and Black's is closer to queening. Only one move holds.
ex.e12.hint: Your rook has two jobs: helping your pawn and stopping the c-pawn. Which move keeps it free for the second one?
ex.e12.solution: 1.f6! The pawn advances on its own and the rook stays free on the h-file. If 1...c3, the rook goes to h8 and checks on d8, and gets behind the c-pawn. If 1...Rf5, then 2.Rf3. 1.Rf3 straight away, behind your own pawn, looks like Tarrasch's rule but loses: 1...c3, and the c-pawn runs while the white rook is tied to the f-file. From a study by Audax6.
ex.e13: White to move and win. Yusupov against Timman, 1992. Your a-pawn is passed. Where does the rook work best?
ex.e13.hint: Behind the pawn the rook protects only one thing. Look for a square where it protects more than one pawn.
ex.e13.solution: 35.Re4! From the fourth rank the rook protects the a-pawn from the side and the f-pawn at the same time. The black rook stays tied to the a-pawn, and the white king is free to advance. 35.Ra1, behind the pawn, was the game move: the rook had only the a-pawn to look after, and the game was drawn twenty moves later. It is an exception to Tarrasch's rule.
ex.e14: White to move and win. Unzicker against Lundin, 1954. The black rook is behind your pawn and the black king threatens to break into your kingside. Only one move wins.
ex.e14.hint: Pushing the pawn is the plan, but first think: after a check on a2, where would the black king go?
ex.e14.solution: 48.f3+! Only this move wins. The check drives the black king away from your kingside, and only then comes 49.a7. If 48.a7 at once, 48...Ra2+ and the black king gets to f3: it attacks your pawns and the defence holds. After 48.f3+ and 49.a7, the black rook can only watch the pawn, and the white king walks over to it. With the black pawn still on f7, the king could go back to f6 or g7, and it would be a draw.
ex.e15: White to move and win. Your f-pawn is one step from queening, but the black rook is behind it. Think before you promote.
ex.e15.hint: The black rook holds the pawn only along the f-file. How can your rook cut that file?
ex.e15.solution: 1.Rb5! The threat is 2.Rf5: your rook steps between the black rook and the pawn, and the pawn queens. If 1...Re2+, 2.Re5! blocks the check and 3.Rf5 follows. If the rook takes on f7, the king recaptures and your rook catches the black pawns with 3.Rb4. The hasty 1.f8=Q? only draws: 1...Rxf8 2.Rxf8 Kb3, and the black king with the pawns holds. From a study by Audax6.
key.behind: The white rook is behind the passed pawn, the black rook in front of it. With every step of the pawn the white rook gains room and the black one gets more stuck: White wins.
key.front: The same pieces with the rooks swapped: now it is the white rook that is stuck in front of the pawn. A draw.
key.defend: Now the passed pawn is Black's. The white rook goes behind it and draws; staying in front loses.
key.race: Both rooks are fighting for the square behind the pawn. The white rook has to find the right route to get there first: only one wins.
key.alekhine: World Championship 1927, Alekhine against Capablanca: the white rook behind the pawn tied the black rook down in front of it, and the white king went after the pawns on the other side. It was the last game of the match.
key.anand: Anand against Kramnik, World Championship 2007: the white rook went behind the black pawn, and the pawn never got through. A draw.
key.kramnik: Kramnik against Beliavsky, 1993: putting the rook behind his own pawn was the losing move, because the danger was the black pawns.
history: When a passed pawn races to promote, the rook works better behind it than in front of it: behind, it gains space with every step the pawn takes; in front, it gets stuck. The rule holds for your own pawn and for your opponent's too. It bears the name of Siegbert Tarrasch (1862–1934), one of the strongest players of his time and such a good teacher that in Germany he was called "the teacher of Germany". He wrote it down in his book on the great St. Petersburg tournament of 1914, commenting on a game between Marshall and Lasker. The rule has famous exceptions, such as Kramnik against Beliavsky in 1993, which is why it is worth understanding why it works rather than just memorising it.
practice: Now the practical challenge: your rook behind the pawn, the black rook in front of it. Bring the king forward and win.
step.d_switch: The black king has reached b5 and blocks your king's way to the a-pawn. Do what Alekhine did: switch targets.
step.d_switch.m1: 1.Kd4! The king heads for the kingside. The a5 pawn does not need it: your rook protects it from behind.
step.d_switch.m2: 1...Rd6+. The black rook leaves the front of the pawn to give checks.
step.d_switch.m3: 2.Ke5. The king attacks the rook and keeps heading for g6.
step.d_switch.m4: 2...Rd1. The rook backs off; the black king cannot take a5, which your rook protects.
step.d_switch.m5: 3.Kf6. The king closes in on the g6 pawn, which stands alone.
step.d_switch.m6: 3...Rd6+. Checks from the side only delay things.
step.d_switch.m7: 4.Kg5. The king steps out of check and attacks g6.
step.d_switch.m8: 4...Rd1. Nothing protects g6: the black king is tied to the a-pawn.
step.d_switch.m9: 5.Kxg6. The g-pawn falls, and now you have two passers. That is what Alekhine did with 62.Kd4.
